'''''Riccia''''' is a genus of [[Marchantiophyta|liverwort]]s in the order [[Marchantiales]].<ref name="Schuster">{{cite book 
| last=Schuster | first=Rudolf M. | year=1992 
| title=The Hepaticae and Anthocerotae of North America | volume=VI | pages=421–440 
| location=Chicago | publisher=Field Museum of Natural History | isbn=0-914868-21-7 }}</ref>

==Description==
These plants are small and [[thallus|thalloid]], i.e. not differentiated into root, stem and leaf. Depending on species, the thallus may be strap-shaped and about 0.5 to 4 mm wide with dichotomous branches or may form [[rosette (botany)|rosettes]] or hemirosettes up to 3 cm in diameter, that may be gregarious and form intricate mats.<ref name=Schuster /><ref name="bbsfieldguide">{{cite book |editor1-last=Atherton |editor1-first=Ian |editor2-last=Bosanquet |editor2-first=Sam |editor3-last=Lawley |editor3-first=Mark |date=2010 |title=Mosses and liverworts of Britain and Ireland: a field guide |location=UK |publisher=British Bryological Society|pages=261–270|isbn=978-0956131010}}</ref>

The thallus is [[dorsiventral]]ly differentiated. Its upper (dorsal) surface is green and [[chlorophyll]]-bearing, with a mid-dorsal longitudinal sulcus (furrow or groove). Air pores occasionally break through the dorsal surface, giving the thallus a dimpled appearance. In exceptional members such as ''Riccia caroliniana'' <ref>Na-Thalang, O., 1980. A revision of the genus Riccia (Hepaticae) in Australia. Brunonia, 3(1), pp. 61–140.</ref><ref>Cargill, D.C., Neal, W.C., Sharma, I. and Gueidan, C., 2016. A preliminary molecular phylogeny of the genus Riccia L.(Ricciaceae) in Australia. Australian Systematic Botany, 29(3), pp. 197–217.</ref> of Northern Australia and ''Riccia sahyadrica'' <ref>Cargill, D.C., Manju, C.N., Deepa, K.M., Chandini, V.K. and Rajesh, K.P. 2019. A New Indian Species of Riccia with connections to Northern Australia. Journal of Bryology 42, DOI. https://doi.org/10.1080/03736687.2019.1611249</ref> of Western Ghats, the photosynthetic region is confined to the lower half of the thallus.<ref name=MacVicar />

The lower (ventral) surface has a mid-ventral ridge bearing multicellular scales that originate as a single row but normally separate into two rows as the thallus widens. The scales are multicellular and [[hyaline]] (glassy) in appearance, or violet due to the pigment [[anthocyanin]].<ref name=Schuster />

[[Rhizoid]]s are nearly lacking in aquatic forms, but there are usually numerous unicellular rhizoids of two types on the ventral surface.<ref name=Schuster /> One type is called smooth and the other type is the pegged or tuberculated rhizoids; these help in anchorage and absorption. The inner surface of the smooth rhizoids is smooth while that of the tuberculate rhizoid will have internal [[cell wall]] projections.

==Distribution and habitat==
One of the more than 100 species in this genus is the "slender riccia" (''[[Riccia fluitans]]''), which grows on damp soil or, less commonly, floating in ponds,<ref name=MacVicar>MacVicar, Symers M. 1971. The student's handbook of British hepatics, p. 12-13. Hitchen Whelden & Wesley, Ltd.; Authorized reprint of the 1926 edition published by Sumfield & Day, Ltd.</ref> and is sometimes used in [[aquarium]]s.

==Reproduction==
Plants are usually [[monoicous]], and sexual reproduction is by [[antheridium|antheridia]] and [[archegonium|archegonia]]. Asexual reproduction occurs by [[spores]], by fragmentation of the rosettes, and by formation of apical [[tubers]]. Spores are large (45 to 200 [[micron|μ]]) and formed in tetrads.<ref name=Schuster />

The [[sporophyte]] of Riccia is the simplest amongst [[bryophyte]]s. It consists of only a capsule, missing both foot and seta, and does not perform photosynthesis.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=xNQE_89dat8C&dq=The+simplest+known+sporophyte+among+bryophytes+is+that+of+Riccia.&pg=PA443 Text Book Of Botany Diversity Of Microbes And Cryptogams]</ref>
